social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband and two children

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive hand and foot numbness, unsteady gait, and profound fatigue for 18 months
patient.history_present_illness: A 45-year-old elementary school librarian with autoimmune gastritis and Hashimoto's hypothyroidism presented to neurology clinic with an 18-month history of progressive bilateral hand and foot numbness, unsteady gait, and profound fatigue. She was diagnosed with pernicious anemia two weeks ago by her internist after her CBC showed macrocytic anemia and her B12 level was critically low (52 pg/mL). She was started on oral cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg daily two weeks ago. Her neurological symptoms began approximately 18 months ago with tingling in her fingertips bilaterally, which she attributed to typing at work. Over the following months the tingling spread to both feet and her balance gradually worsened. For the past 6 months she has been unsteady on her feet, particularly on the stairs and in the dark, and has had four near-falls. She reports profound fatigue and difficulty with concentration — her colleagues have noticed she is slower and makes more mistakes than usual. She has noticed difficulty with fine motor tasks — she drops items, has difficulty with needlepoint (a hobby she has had for 20 years), and her handwriting has deteriorated. She did not connect these neurological symptoms to a B12 problem until her diagnosis two weeks ago. On direct questioning she also endorses occasional electric-shock sensations down her spine when she bends her neck forward — Lhermitte's sign. She denies bowel or bladder symptoms.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x3. Slightly slowed processing. Mild word-finding difficulty. Mini-cog normal. She appears pale.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild bilateral intrinsic hand weakness (4+/5 grip, 4/5 APB). Mild bilateral finger extensor weakness (4+/5). Lower extremities: normal strength. No wasting.
neurological_exam.sensory: Severe proprioceptive loss bilateral hands and feet — cannot detect small movements. Vibration severely reduced at bilateral fingertips, wrists, ankles, and great toes. Light touch and pinprick mildly reduced in stocking distribution. Lhermitte's sign: electric sensation down spine on neck flexion — positive.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Ankle reflexes absent bilaterally. Biceps and brachioradialis 1+. Knee jerks 1+. Plantar flexors bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Heel-shin: moderately ataxic. Finger-nose: moderately inaccurate bilateral (proprioceptive).
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based sensory ataxia. Romberg markedly positive. Cannot tandem walk.
neurological_exam.additional: Pale skin and conjunctivae (anemia). Smooth, atrophic tongue (glossitis). No hepatosplenomegaly.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: Hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL (L), MCV 118 fL (H), Hypersegmented neutrophils Present (5-lobed neutrophils)  (H), Vitamin B12 52 pg/mL (L), MMA 1.84 umol/L (H), Homocysteine 42 umol/L (H), Anti-parietal cell antibodies Strongly positive (1:320)  (H), Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies Positive  (H).

specialized_test.test_type: Nerve conduction studies and EMG — bilateral upper and lower extremities

findings.pattern: Mildly reduced amplitude — upper extremity involvement

quantitative_data.pattern: Predominantly large-fiber sensory axonal neuropathy — SNAP reductions without motor involvement; consistent with subacute combined degeneration affecting posterior columns + peripheral nerves

specialized_test.impression: Predominantly large-fiber sensory neuropathy (reduced SNAP amplitudes bilaterally in upper and lower extremities; motor NCS normal). EMG normal — no denervation. This pattern, combined with critically low B12, positive Lhermitte's sign, and severe proprioceptive/vibration loss, is consistent with subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (SCDC) from B12 deficiency. MRI spine is urgently required to assess posterior column involvement.
recommended_actions: MRI cervical and thoracic spine (sagittal T2) — posterior column signal change assessment
Switch to IM cyanocobalamin given pernicious anemia (oral absorption requires intrinsic factor)
Urgent hematology referral for pernicious anemia management

output.impression: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (SCDC) — bilateral posterior column T2 hyperintensity in cervical and thoracic cord. 'Inverted V sign' on axial T2 is characteristic. Urgent optimization of B12 replacement required. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.proposed: IM cyanocobalamin for pernicious anemia with subacute combined degeneration
warnings: CRITICAL: Pernicious anemia patients cannot absorb oral B12 due to intrinsic factor deficiency — oral therapy is insufficient; IM injections are required
Standard protocol: 1000 mcg IM daily x 7 days, then 1000 mcg weekly x 4 weeks, then 1000 mcg monthly for life
Neurological improvement expected in 3-6 months but may be incomplete if diagnosis delayed
alternatives: Hydroxocobalamin IM — alternative to cyanocobalamin, longer duration

results.title: Autoimmune gastritis and gastric cancer risk — surveillance recommendations
results.key_finding: Autoimmune atrophic gastritis (pernicious anemia) carries 3-4x increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric carcinoid; upper endoscopy recommended at diagnosis and every 3-5 years

output.summary: Autoimmune gastritis (anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies positive) carries increased gastric cancer risk. Upper endoscopy (EGD) is recommended at diagnosis and every 3-5 years. Gastroenterology referral required.

findings.finding: Mild cardiovagal dysfunction — HRV mildly reduced. No significant orthostatic hypotension.

output.impression: Mild autonomic involvement from B12 deficiency — consistent with subacute combined degeneration affecting autonomic fibers. Expected to improve with B12 replacement.

output.query: B12 deficiency subacute combined degeneration treatment prognosis

results.title: Neurological outcomes of B12 deficiency with SCDC
results.key_finding: Neurological improvement with IM B12 is expected within 3-6 months; improvement is better in patients treated early; posterior column MRI changes may normalize with treatment; incomplete improvement is common if duration >12 months before treatment

output.summary: Prognosis for neurological recovery: partial improvement expected within 3-6 months of adequate IM B12 therapy. The posterior column T2 signal changes on MRI may normalize over months to years. Given 18-month duration before diagnosis, complete recovery is unlikely but significant functional improvement is expected. Lifelong monthly IM B12 maintenance is required for pernicious anemia.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (SCDC) from vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia)

differential.key_features: Lhermitte's sign and posterior column signal on MRI can occur in MS; however B12 52 pg/mL critically low with strongly positive anti-intrinsic factor Ab — pernicious anemia is the primary diagnosis; MS would require additional lesions and full diagnostic criteria
Posterior column involvement with Lhermitte's and sensory ataxia — similar pattern; however RPR non-reactive and B12 critically low
HbA1c 5.2% — no diabetes. B12 deficiency is the primary etiology.
Lhermitte's sign and posterior column symptoms could suggest cervical pathology; however MRI shows posterior column T2 signal without compressive lesion — SCDC pattern confirmed

critical_actions: Switch to IM cyanocobalamin IMMEDIATELY — pernicious anemia requires IM therapy (oral is insufficient without intrinsic factor)
NEVER treat B12 deficiency with folate alone — neurological degeneration (SCDC) continues while hematological signs mask
MRI spine urgently — posterior column involvement confirms SCDC and guides prognosis
Gastric cancer surveillance (EGD) is mandatory in autoimmune gastritis/pernicious anemia
Lifelong monthly IM B12 is required — this is not a temporary deficiency
contraindicated_actions: Continuing oral B12 supplementation for pernicious anemia — intrinsic factor deficiency means oral absorption is insufficient; IM required
Treating with folate alone without B12 — masks hematology but neurological damage progresses
Attributing Lhermitte's sign to cervical spondylosis without checking B12 in a patient with pernicious anemia markers
key_reasoning_points: B12 52 pg/mL critically low with MMA 1.84 and Hcy 42 confirms severe functional deficiency
Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies confirm pernicious anemia — oral B12 absorption is blocked; IM required
Lhermitte's sign and MRI posterior column T2 confirm SCDC — spinal cord involvement, not just peripheral neuropathy
The dominant neurological picture is large-fiber sensory (proprioception/vibration) — the hallmark of SCDC from B12 deficiency
Autoimmune gastritis requires gastric cancer surveillance regardless of neurological recovery

red_herrings.data_point: Lhermitte's sign (electric shock sensation on neck flexion) in a 45-year-old woman
red_herrings.intended_effect: Multiple sclerosis suspected as primary diagnosis, delaying B12 deficiency treatment
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Lhermitte's sign is not specific to MS — it can occur in SCDC from B12 deficiency. With B12 52 pg/mL critically low and MRI showing posterior column T2 (SCDC pattern), pernicious anemia is the primary diagnosis.

red_herrings.data_point: Oral cyanocobalamin started 2 weeks ago for pernicious anemia
red_herrings.intended_effect: B12 replacement considered adequate — continued on oral without switching to IM
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Pernicious anemia is caused by intrinsic factor deficiency — oral B12 cannot be adequately absorbed without intrinsic factor. IM cyanocobalamin is required for lifelong pernicious anemia management.

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Straightforward B12 deficiency neuropathy with subacute combined degeneration — pernicious anemia with critically low B12, anti-intrinsic factor antibodies, MRI posterior column changes; IM vs oral B12 as critical management point.
